title: One year of the euro revealed where currency union had integrated markets
summary: Sirkka Hämäläinen judged that the euro’s first year had created a functioning area-wide money market and an important international currency of issuance, while leaving investors, collateral markets and retail banking considerably more segmented. Her 8 January speech offers an assessment of how far market integration had progressed after twelve months. Its argument for the single currency rests on domestic purchasing power, competition and financing costs over time. The external exchange rate could fluctuate before those benefits emerged. At the speech date euro banknotes and coins were still due to arrive in 2002, so the effects on price comparisons and competition in shops remained prospective.

The operational test was whether one policy decision could transmit across eleven participating countries. The Eurosystem drew on national central banks’ experience with their counterparties while using a common, flexible framework and a broad collateral base. Hämäläinen credits that flexibility for the smooth century date change without special instruments or facilities. In the unsecured interbank market, cross-border settlement through TARGET made it possible to move funds between countries and exploit differences in money-market rates. The result, in her assessment, was a largely integrated market within a short period. She regarded institutional independence and the ability to implement decisions throughout the area as sources of policy credibility (the first and third observations on the euro’s first year).

Her international evidence draws an important distinction between borrowers and investors. Preliminary figures put euro-denominated bonds at around 40–45% of new international issue volume in the first three quarters of 1999, close to the dollar share over that interval. This was an issuance flow over nine months, not the euro’s share of outstanding global portfolios or reserves. More than 50 European and African countries had exchange arrangements linked in various ways to the euro or to baskets in which it had an important weight. These arrangements differed in design. Despite those signs of international use, she saw less corresponding enthusiasm from investors. Fragmented capital markets and uncertainty over structural policies gave investors reasons to wait. No comparable investor allocation series was supplied to quantify the difference.

For an investor seeking to finance or hedge a position, the contrast between unsecured funding and repo was revealing. Banks could transfer cash across borders, yet secured funding depended on which bonds qualified, their credit risk and liquidity, the legal terms of the repo, and the capacity to deliver collateral across settlement systems. At the time she counted 29 securities settlement systems in the euro area. Building links for simultaneous settlement of the securities and cash legs involved costs that inhibited adoption. This left room for a feedback loop: more issuance and trading could justify investment in common infrastructure, which could make later cross-border trading cheaper. It also left open how long the market would remain divided while participants waited for sufficient volume (discussion of repo and settlement).

Integration differed within bond markets too. Government issuers had increasingly converged on common issuance practices, with larger average deals and more competition in secondary trading. The German Pfandbrief model was spreading to other markets, including France and Spain. Larger benchmark issues could improve liquidity. Corporate bond issuance had grown and reached a broader set of credit qualities, including lower-rated issuers. She considered that development promising for innovative smaller companies’ future access to finance. The remarks document issuance by a wider range of institutions. They do not establish that small growth firms had already obtained widespread direct market funding or that existing pricing reflected a permanent reduction in risk.

The remaining work involved governments, European institutions and private market organisations. Compatible legal documentation, cross-border collateral rules, capital raising, pension supervision and restructuring procedures all mattered. Retail banks still offered limited pan-European services. The speaker expected competition and the introduction of cash euros to speed improvement, while leaving the outcome dependent on policy and commercial decisions. Smaller economies such as Finland might gain disproportionately from wider funding markets and more competition in industries dominated by a few local firms. Credibility gains also depended on continued fiscal discipline and structural reform, particularly in large member states. For portfolios, the first year’s evidence therefore supported a differentiated assessment of funding, collateral and investor demand across market segments, with limited grounds for a uniform convergence assumption.

questions.question: Was the new-issue share matched by persistent demand from investors outside the euro area?
questions.detail: A currency can attract issuers for financing or hedging reasons before global investors increase unhedged holdings. Compare the contemporaneous international issuance statistics cited in the speech with investor allocation, secondary turnover and currency hedging data where available. Distinguish gross new deals from net issuance and the outstanding stock. Those distinctions are essential to a view on demand for euro-denominated duration.

questions.question: Which cross-border collateral costs survived after the cash market integrated?
questions.detail: The address names documentation, settlement and the underlying securities as frictions. It does not quantify their separate effects. Compare matched repos against the same or economically similar collateral, controlling for term, counterparty and settlement location. Consult dated Eurosystem collateral rules, market agreements and settlement-system fee schedules. The answer determines how far unsecured rate convergence carries over to the financing cost of a relative-value bond position.

questions.question: Did integration reach the cost of capital for smaller companies?
questions.detail: A broader set of issuers and larger benchmark transactions can improve capital-market depth without materially changing funding for smaller firms. Compare the size and rating of actual new issuers with firms still dependent on domestic banks. Published issuance records, loan pricing and firm-level accounts could test whether the benefits reached borrowers beyond the most established names and whether access varied by country.
